newsitem.title: USA: Clinton urged to arrest all Bosnian war criminals.
newsitem.headline: Clinton urged to arrest all Bosnian war criminals.

text.p: President Bill Clinton came under pressure on Tuesday from key politicians and more than 80 groups who insisted he take the lead in ensuring all Bosnian war criminals are brought to justice.

"If we do not arrest the perpetrators of these crimes of genocide we will risk the investment of billions of dollars -- right now it's about $7 billion -- thousands of military and civilian personnel and our prestige and influence as the greatest country on the face of the earth," former Republican presidential nominee Bob Dole said.
Also, "we will not ultimately achieve peace in that country," he said.

"This is where strong presidential leadership will come into play ... This must be the beginning of a full-time effort to bring war criminals to justice," said Dole, the former Senate majority leader.

Dole and Democratic Sen. Joseph Lieberman headlined a news conference sponsored by the Coalition for International Justice, linking more than 80 religious, labour, ethnic, women's and human rights groups in a campaign to force the U.S. government to act.

The group published an open letter to Clinton in the New York Times on Tuesday in which they expressed distress that indicted war criminals were living freely and said by not allowing its soldiers to arrest suspects, the United States may have "colluded" in protecting these individuals.
Lieberman acknowledged that pursuing war criminals was risky for NATO-led peacekeepers in Bosnia.
But he insisted bringing them to justice was a matter of principle and if Clinton took a firm position in support of such action, the American people would support him.
While the NATO-led troops have authority to arrest the 76 suspects indicted for war crimes by the international tribunal in the Hague, they had not used that power until last week.
The arrest operation was carried out on Thursday near the northwestern town of Prijedor by British special forces acting on orders from North Atlantic Treaty Organisation commanders.
British troops snatched one suspect, who was later transported to the Hague by the United States, and a second suspect was killed when he fired on British forces.
Lieberman said he believed that as a result of this operation "the (U.S.) policy is changing."

In connection with the snatch, Clinton warned Bosnian Serbs on Tuesday against retaliation. "They have no call to take any retaliatory action and it would be a grave mistake to do so," Clinton told reporters at the White House.

He expressed concern about a Bosnian Serb backlash after the NATO arrest, but said the snatch was warranted because Bosnian Serbs have not honoured their Dayton peace accords pledge to turn over indicted war criminals to the Hague.

Clinton commented after a bomb explosion early on Tuesday outside the apartment of an international monitor in Bosnian Serb-controlled territory, the second night the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) was targeted.
Dole and Lieberman made separate recent visits to Bosnia.

They told similar incidents about U.S. officials who encounter the Mercedes-Benz car of Radovan Karadzic -- chief wartime leader of the Bosnian Serbs and the leading suspect indicted for wear crimes -- outside official buildings in Pale, the Bosnian Serb headquarters, when they are enroute to meetings with Bosnian Serb leaders.

"Sometimes they (U.S. officials) are stopped at the door and asked to wait a few minutes and what they realise is happening is that Karadzic is going out the backdoor to get in his car and leave," Lieberman said.

Noting that France controls the zone of Bosnia that includes Pale, Lieberman and Dole both said the French had a major role to play in apprehending Karadzic and other indicted war criminals who inhabit that area. But the United States must also be involved, they said.
